subject_meta_title: Personal Allowance 2026/27: How Much You Can Earn Tax-Free
subject_meta_description: The UK Personal Allowance for 2026/27, when it starts to shrink above £100,000, and the income at which it disappears completely.
label: Standard Personal Allowance
context: The amount of income most people can receive each tax year before paying any Income Tax. It applies across the whole UK, including Scotland.

label: Allowance starts to reduce above
context: For every £2 of adjusted net income above this, the Personal Allowance falls by £1.

label: Allowance is lost completely at
context: At this level of adjusted net income the taper has removed the whole allowance, so all income is taxable.

subject_name: Income Tax Rates and Bands (England, Wales and NI)
subject_intro: The Income Tax rates paid on earnings, pensions and other non-savings income outside Scotland, and the income levels where each rate starts.
subject_meta_title: Income Tax Rates and Bands 2026/27 (England, Wales and NI)
subject_meta_description: Current UK Income Tax rates: 20% basic, 40% higher and 45% additional, with the income thresholds for each band in 2026/27.
label: Basic rate
context: Paid on taxable income above the Personal Allowance, up to the higher rate threshold.

label: Higher rate starts above
context: Income above this level is taxed at the higher rate, assuming the standard Personal Allowance.

label: Higher rate
context: Paid on income between the higher rate threshold and the additional rate threshold.

label: Additional rate starts above
context: Income above this level is taxed at the additional rate. By this point the Personal Allowance has been fully withdrawn.

label: Additional rate
context: The top rate of Income Tax outside Scotland.
Income up to this amount is taxed at 0% before the basic rate applies.

subject_name: Scottish Income Tax Rates and Bands
subject_intro: Scotland sets its own Income Tax rates and bands on earnings, pensions and other non-savings income, with six bands instead of three.
subject_meta_title: Scottish Income Tax Rates and Bands 2026/27
subject_meta_description: All six Scottish Income Tax rates for 2026/27, from the 19% starter rate to the 48% top rate, and the income level where each band begins.
label: Starter rate
context: Paid on the first slice of income above the Personal Allowance, up to £16,537.

label: Basic rate starts at
context: Gross income, assuming the standard Personal Allowance. Raised for 2026/27.

label: Basic rate
context: Paid on income from the basic rate threshold up to £29,526.

label: Intermediate rate starts at
context: Gross income, assuming the standard Personal Allowance. Raised for 2026/27.

label: Intermediate rate
context: Paid on income from the intermediate rate threshold up to £43,662.

label: Higher rate starts at
context: Gross income, assuming the standard Personal Allowance.

label: Higher rate
context: Paid on income from the higher rate threshold up to £75,000.

label: Advanced rate starts at
context: Gross income, assuming the standard Personal Allowance.

label: Advanced rate
context: Paid on income from the advanced rate threshold up to £125,140.

label: Top rate applies over
context: The same level at which the Personal Allowance is fully withdrawn.

label: Top rate
context: The highest rate of Scottish Income Tax.
Scottish taxpayers get the same UK-wide Personal Allowance before the starter rate applies.

subcategory_description: National Insurance rates and thresholds for employees, employers and the self-employed.
subject_intro: What employees pay in Class 1 National Insurance on their wages, the thresholds where it starts and falls, and what employers pay on top.
subject_meta_description: Class 1 National Insurance for 2026/27: 8% for employees between £12,570 and £50,270, 2% above, and 15% for employers above £5,000.
label: Employee main rate
context: Paid on earnings between the Primary Threshold and the Upper Earnings Limit, for most employees (category A).

label: Primary Threshold (yearly)
context: Employees pay no National Insurance on earnings up to this level. The weekly equivalent is £242.

label: Upper Earnings Limit (yearly)
context: Above this, the employee rate drops to 2%. The weekly equivalent is £967.

label: Employee rate above the Upper Earnings Limit
Lower Earnings Limit (weekly)
context: Earning at least this much a week builds entitlement to the State Pension and some benefits, even though no National Insurance is paid until the Primary Threshold.

label: Employer rate
context: Paid by employers on earnings above the Secondary Threshold, with no upper limit.

label: Secondary Threshold (yearly)
context: Employers start paying National Insurance on an employee's earnings above this level. The weekly equivalent is £96.

subject_intro: Class 4 National Insurance on self-employed profits, and when voluntary Class 2 contributions are worth paying to protect your State Pension record.
subject_meta_description: Class 4 National Insurance for 2026/27: 6% on profits between £12,570 and £50,270, 2% above, plus the Class 2 thresholds and voluntary rate.
label: Class 4 main rate
context: Paid through Self Assessment on profits between the Lower and Upper Profits Limits.

label: Lower Profits Limit
context: No Class 4 National Insurance is due on profits up to this level.

label: Upper Profits Limit
context: Above this, the Class 4 rate drops to 2%.

label: Class 4 rate above the Upper Profits Limit
Small Profits Threshold
context: With profits at or above this level, Class 2 contributions are treated as paid, so the year counts towards the State Pension at no cost.

label: Voluntary Class 2 rate (weekly)
context: Optional for those with profits below the Small Profits Threshold who want to protect their National Insurance record.

subcategory_description: Capital Gains Tax and dividend tax rates and allowances for individual investors.
subject_name: Capital Gains Tax Rates and Allowance
subject_intro: The tax-free allowance for capital gains and the rates paid on gains above it, including Business Asset Disposal Relief.
subject_meta_title: Capital Gains Tax Rates and Allowance 2026/27
subject_meta_description: Capital Gains Tax for 2026/27: the £3,000 annual exempt amount, 18% and 24% rates, and the 18% Business Asset Disposal Relief rate.
label: Annual tax-free allowance
context: Gains up to this amount in a tax year are free of Capital Gains Tax for individuals.

label: Rate within the basic rate band
context: Applies to the part of a gain that fits within any unused basic rate band once income is taken into account. The same rate applies to residential property and other assets.

label: Rate above the basic rate band
context: Applies to gains above the basic rate band, and to all gains for higher and additional rate taxpayers.

label: Business Asset Disposal Relief rate
context: The rate on qualifying gains when selling all or part of a business. It rose from 14% on 6 April 2026.

label: Business Asset Disposal Relief lifetime limit
context: The total qualifying gains that can benefit from the relief over a lifetime.

subject_intro: How much tax is paid on dividends from shares held outside an ISA, and the tax-free dividend allowance.
subject_meta_description: Dividend tax for 2026/27: the £500 dividend allowance and the 10.75%, 35.75% and 39.35% rates that apply above it.
label: Dividend allowance
context: The first £500 of dividend income each tax year is tax-free, whatever your tax band. Dividends inside an ISA don't count.

label: Basic rate on dividends
context: Up from 8.75% on 6 April 2026. Scottish taxpayers use these UK dividend rates too.

label: Higher rate on dividends
context: Up from 33.75% on 6 April 2026.

label: Additional rate on dividends
context: Unchanged for 2026/27.

subcategory_description: Inheritance Tax thresholds, rates and allowances on estates.
subject_intro: How much an estate can pass on before Inheritance Tax is due, the extra allowance for passing on a home, and the rates charged above the thresholds.
subject_meta_description: UK Inheritance Tax: the £325,000 nil-rate band, the £175,000 residence nil-rate band, and the 40% rate, or 36% when leaving to charity.
label: Nil-rate band
context: Estates below this value normally pay no Inheritance Tax. Any unused amount can pass to a surviving spouse or civil partner.

label: Residence nil-rate band
context: An extra allowance when a home is left to children or grandchildren, taking the potential tax-free amount to £500,000.

label: Residence allowance starts to reduce above
context: For estates worth more than this, the residence nil-rate band falls by £1 for every £2 over.

label: Standard rate
context: Charged on the part of the estate above the available thresholds.

label: Reduced rate when leaving to charity
context: Applies when at least 10% of the net estate is left to charity.

subcategory_description: Property purchase taxes across the UK: Stamp Duty Land Tax in England and Northern Ireland, LBTT in Scotland and LTT in Wales.
subject_intro: In Scotland, Land and Buildings Transaction Tax replaces Stamp Duty. These are the residential rates, first-time buyer relief and the supplement on additional homes.
subject_meta_description: LBTT residential rates in Scotland: nil to £145,000 (£175,000 for first-time buyers), bands of 2% to 12%, and the 8% Additional Dwelling Supplement.
label: Nil-rate threshold
context: No LBTT is due on the first £145,000 of a standard residential purchase.

label: Rate on £145,001 to £250,000
context: Each rate applies only to the part of the price within that band.

label: First-time buyer nil-rate threshold
context: First-time buyer relief raises the nil-rate band, saving up to £600.

label: Additional Dwelling Supplement
context: Charged on the whole price, on top of LBTT, when buying an additional home such as a buy-to-let or second home.
For comparison: the equivalent nil-rate threshold for Stamp Duty in England and Northern Ireland.

subject_intro: In Wales, Land Transaction Tax replaces Stamp Duty. These are the main residential rates and the higher rates for buyers who already own a property.
subject_meta_description: LTT residential rates in Wales: nil to £225,000, main rates of 6% to 12%, and higher rates from 5% to 17% for additional properties.
label: Nil-rate threshold
context: No LTT is due on the first £225,000 of a main-rate residential purchase. Wales has no separate first-time buyer relief.

label: Rate on £225,001 to £400,000
context: Each rate applies only to the part of the price within that band.

label: Higher rates: first £180,000
context: Higher rates usually apply when buying a residential property worth £40,000 or more while already owning another.

label: Higher rates: above £1.5m
context: The top higher-rate band, rising in steps from 5% through 8.5%, 10%, 12.5% and 15%.
For comparison: the equivalent nil-rate threshold for Stamp Duty in England and Northern Ireland.
